# Setup

### **q1** Planning a study (TEAMWORK)

While you provided this plan in c08 (Part 1), please include your plan here. In particular, describe how you updated your plan in response to feedback.

#### Population

- Our population is all adult islanders (age 18+). However, we will only be randomly selecting islanders from a total of 12 cities across the three islands.

#### Quantity of interest

- We are going to examine people's relationship histories across the three islands. In particular, we are measuring the number of relationships islanders have been in (only looking at relationships they have had when they were 18+), length of relationships, and whether they got married.

#### Covariates

- The age of the person (if they are older, they have had more time to be in relationships). We can control for this by calculating a relationships/year variable.
- The population size of each island and each city could affect the relationships islanders get into.
- One thing we have to consider is that islanders may move between the islands. We are assuming this will happen infrequently, and we will just count an islander who has moved as living on the island they are currently living on.

#### Observation or experiment?

- Observational study.

#### Question / Hypothesis

- How do dating and marriage histories vary across islands?
- Null hypothesis: There is no difference in dating patterns between islands.
- Alternative hypothesis: There are differences in dating (such as relationship lengths, number of relationships, etc) between different islands.

#### Sampling plan

- We will assign each of our four team members one city from each island, and from each city each team member will collect data on ten people. In total, this will result in a sample of 40 people from each island and 120 people total from all islands.

- Within each city, we will generate 10 random numbers to choose the household that we collect data from. If a house has multiple people that are 18+ years old, we will randomly choose one person from the household to sample. If the house has no residents 18+, we will randomly select a new one.

- In each house, we will collect the number of relationships, how long they lasted, and whether they got married or not.

- Within our data collection spreadsheet, we will have one row per relationship. This means one individual may have several rows. We chose to do it this way so that each row has the same number of columns, as opposed to having one row per islander in which case we would need a column for each relationship they are in resulting in each row having a variable number of columns.

- The columns will be: Name, Age, House, City, Island, Birth island, Relationships, Married

- We're trying to make it more representative of the general population by doing random sampling, plus taking samples across cities adds more diversity as well. Of course, we can't make it perfectly representative, since it's a limited number of people and cities, but we're trying to ensure diversity.

- Choice of sample size: 157

  (Feasibility) We thought 40 people per island, which is 30 people per students and 120 total would be a reasonable amount of islanders to sample in terms of having a reasonable number of people for each student to go through. A larger sample would probably give us more precise results, but would also take longer.

  \
  (Power analysis) We performed a power analysis using the site ZDR showed in class ([https://www.statscalculators.com/calculators/hypothesis-testing/sample-size-and-power-analysis-calculator).](https://www.statscalculators.com/calculators/hypothesis-testing/sample-size-and-power-analysis-calculator).) The study design we chose was comparing several group means because we are comparing characteristics of islanders from three different islands.

  Here are our parameter choices:

  - Significance level (α) = 0.05: This is a standard choice for confidence level. There are no particular reasons we would need a higher confidence level for this study.

  - Target power = 0.8: Also a standard choice. There is no reason that missing a difference between the islands would be costly, so we don’t need to have a higher target power than the standard.

  - Cohen’s f = 0.25: This is difficult to justify because we don’t have prior data on how large the effect of living on different islands is on people’s relationship histories within the Islands simulation. However, 0.5 corresponds to being able to detect a “medium” difference according to Cohen’s benchmarks, which seems like a reasonable target for our study since it is just meant to explore differences between the islanders.

  This power analysis resulted in requiring 159 observations for our study. That is just under 40 observations per student, which is a little bit over our original plan of 30 observations per student, but it’s not much more. 

  Taking both the feasibility and power analysis into consideration, we decided on a final sample size of 159. With this sample size, our study should be able to detect a “medium” sized difference between the relationship histories of islanders, and it will be a reasonable amount of work for our team to do.

### **q2** EDA

```{r imports}
library(tidyverse)
df_raw <- read_csv("./data/main_sheet.csv")
```

```{r data-cleaning}
df <- df_raw %>%
  rename(
    name = "Name",
    age = "Age",
    house = "House",
    city = "City",
    island = "Island",
    birth_island = "Birth island",
    relationship_length = "Relationship Length",
    married = "Married"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    relationship_length = case_when(
      relationship_length == "none" ~ NA_real_,
      relationship_length == "<1" ~ 0.5, # so it shows up on a numerical axis
      TRUE ~ as.numeric(relationship_length)
    ),
    married = married == "yes" | married == "Yes",
    island = case_when(
      island == "Bonne Santé" ~ "Bonne Sante",
      TRUE ~ island
    )
  )

df_people <- df %>%
  group_by(name, age, house, city, island, birth_island) %>%
  summarise(
    n_relationships = sum(!is.na(relationship_length)),
    ever_married = any(married),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    age_group = case_when(
      age <= 30 ~ "18-30",
      age <= 45 ~ "31-45",
      age <= 60 ~ "46-60",
      TRUE ~ "61+"
    )
  )
```

```{r plot-1}
df %>%
  ggplot(aes(age, fill = island)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 3, color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~island, ncol = 1) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

```{r plot-2}
df_people %>%
  ggplot(aes(n_relationships, fill = island)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_width(1)) +
  facet_grid(island ~ .)
```

```{r plot-3}
df_short_rel <- df %>%
  filter(!is.na(relationship_length)) %>%
  mutate(short_rel = relationship_length < 1) %>%
  group_by(island) %>%
  summarise(prop_short = mean(short_rel), n = n())

df_short_rel %>%
  ggplot(aes(island, prop_short, fill = island)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("n=", n)), vjust = -0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Proportion of relationships lasting less than 1 year",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Percent"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

```{r plot-4}
df_people %>%
  group_by(age_group) %>%
  summarize(avg_relationships = mean(n_relationships)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group, y = avg_relationships)) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(
    x = "Age group",
    y = "Average number of relationships",
  )
```

```{r plot-5}
df_people %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = n_relationships, color = island)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~island) +
  labs(
    x = "Age",
    y = "Number of relationships",
    color = "Island"
  )
```

```{r plot-6}
df_people %>%
  group_by(age_group) %>% 
  summarize(
    n_married = sum(ever_married),
    n_total = n()
  ) %>% 
  mutate(p_married = n_married / n_total)

df_people %>%
  group_by(age_group, island) %>%
  summarize(
    n_married = sum(ever_married),
    n_total = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(p_married = n_married / n_total) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group, y = p_married, fill = island)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(x = "Age group", y = "percent married", fill = "Island")


df_people  %>%
  filter(birth_island %in% c("Bonne Sante", "Providence", "Ironbard"))  %>%
  group_by(age_group, birth_island) %>%
  summarize(
    n_married = sum(ever_married),
    n_total = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(p_married = n_married / n_total) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group, y = p_married, fill = birth_island)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(x = "Age group", y = "percent married", fill = "Birth Island")
```

```{r plot-7}
df %>%
  filter(!is.na(relationship_length)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(relationship_length, fill = island)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 10, color = "white") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~island, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

```{r plot-8}
df %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(married),
    birth_island %in% c("Bonne Sante", "Ironbard", "Providence")
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(relationship_length)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20) +
  facet_grid(married ~ island) +
  scale_x_log10()
```

### **q3** Key Analyses

Present the key analyses that support your questions / hypotheses. This could include summary statistics (e.g., a proportion of Islanders), grouped summary statistics (e.g., a proportion for group A, and for group B), or visualizations (e.g., a histogram). This section should be short, and every analysis should directly relate to q4.

```{r final-plot-1}
df_people %>%
  ggplot(aes(n_relationships, fill = island)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_width(1)) +
  facet_grid(island ~ .)
```

This is a histogram of the number of relationships islanders have been in in their life, separated by the island they live on. The x axis indicates how many relationships islanders have been in, and the y axis indicates how many islanders have had each number of relationships. There does not appear to be any difference between the islands in how many relationships islanders have been in.

```{r final-plot-2}
df %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(married),
    birth_island %in% c("Bonne Sante", "Ironbard", "Providence")
  ) %>%
  ggplot(aes(relationship_length)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20) +
  facet_grid(married ~ island) +
  scale_x_log10()
```

This graph shows the number of relationships of different lengths, separated by island and by whether they were marriages. Of the relationships that were not marriages, there are a large amount that lasted less than 1 year. There are very few relationships lasting more than 10 years that did not get married. Of the relationships that were marriages, most of them lasted more than 10 years. There seems to be no clear difference between the 3 islands, besides that Bonne Sante had fewer relationships that lasted less than 1 year, but that may be because of our small sample size.

```{r final-plot-3}
df_people %>%
  group_by(age_group) %>% 
  summarize(
    n_married = sum(ever_married),
    n_total = n()
  ) %>% 
  mutate(p_married = n_married / n_total)

df_people %>%
  group_by(age_group, island) %>%
  summarize(
    n_married = sum(ever_married),
    n_total = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(p_married = n_married / n_total) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group, y = p_married, fill = island)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(x = "Age group", y = "percent married", fill = "Island")


df_people  %>%
  filter(birth_island %in% c("Bonne Sante", "Providence", "Ironbard"))  %>%
  group_by(age_group, birth_island) %>%
  summarize(
    n_married = sum(ever_married),
    n_total = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(p_married = n_married / n_total) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age_group, y = p_married, fill = birth_island)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(x = "Age group", y = "percent married", fill = "Birth Island")
```

These graphs explore the marriage rates for each age group (18-30, 31-45, 46-60, 61+), and then further explore whether trends emerge based on current island (top) and birth island (bottom). The x axis, percent married, is the percentage of people within that age group who have been married at least once. Based on this graphing, it seems as if people in or from Bonne Sante begin marriage earlier. In the current island graph, there is a trend upward with percentage of people in that age group that have been married, with the exception of a decrease in the age group 45-60 in Providence and in 61+ in Ironbard. 

```{r final-plot-4}
df_people %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = n_relationships, color = island)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~island) +
  labs(
    x = "Age",
    y = "Number of relationships",
    color = "Island"
  )
```

This graph plots the current ages of islanders versus the total number of relationships they’ve been in. We had expected an upward trend because we thought that people who are older would have had more time to date throughout their lives. However, the data seems to show otherwise. The values are relatively evenly scattered across ages, with the highest numbers roughly around their 40s. This is mostly consistent across islands.

### **q4** Answers

Connect your Key Analyses to your questions / hypotheses. What did you conclude from your study?

- In this study, we did not reject the null hypothesis: we did not find any notable differences in dating patterns between islands. 
- There is no trend of older people having more past relationships (which is what we expected). This is because we only sampled people over 18, and most islanders appear to have the majority of their relationships before they are 18.
